extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists, editors, and writers; educated readers interested in journalistic standards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for newspaper editors and journalists: the personal, professional, ethical and practical qualities that make successful journalism and editors, plus compositional techniques (use of anecdote, historical analogy, descriptive detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the only profession in which versatility is not a disadvantage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The great editor/journalist should be versatile rather than narrowly specialized—able to work across the editorial room, composing room and pressroom; versatility enables the editor to understand and manage the whole enterprise rather than perfecting a single narrow skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor must be able to write and judge writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great editor is by no means the great writer. But he ought to be able to write and must be a judge of writing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor does not have to be the foremost writer but must possess writing ability and a critical eye for prose quality; evaluate submissions, shape copy, and recognize good writing in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of all newspaper functions (managerial grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The newspaper office is a little kingdom. The great editor needs to know and does know every range of it between the editorial room, the composing room and the pressroom... having risen, as it were, step-by-step from the ground floor to the roof.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective editors should understand all departments and workflows, command personnel, and have practical hands-on experience rather than ruling from ignorance; managerial competence and institutional memory matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and critical faculties of the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: “He should be level-headed, yet impressionable; sympathetic, yet self-possessed; able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate; of various knowledge, experience and interest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance sensitivity to ideas and readers with steady judgment; rapidly evaluate information, discriminate worthy material, and draw on wide knowledge and interests when making editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and avoidance of extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: “He should keep to the middle of the road and well in rear of the moving columns.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a measured, moderate editorial stance rather than sensational or extreme positions; maintain perspective and avoid being swept by passing enthusiasms or agitators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of the art and independence from personal advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: “Loving his art—for such it is—for art's sake; getting his sufficiency, along with its independence, in the public approval and patronage, seeking never anything further for himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should serve the craft and the public rather than personal ambition—seek independence through public trust and patronage, not office or private gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness and unselfish devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Disinterestedness being the soul of successful journalism, unselfish devotion to every noble purpose in public and private life, he should say to preferment, as to bribers, 'get behind me, Satan.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism’s core ethical requirement is impartiality and resistance to bribery or corrupt influence; public trust depends on demonstrable disinterest and devotion to noble public purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal journalism must be answerable and trustworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus 'personal journalism' cannot be escaped, and whether the 'one-man power' emanates from the Counting Room or the Editorial Room... it must be clear and answerable, responsive to the common weal, and, above all, trustworthy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because newspapers inevitably have identifiable leaders, those leaders must be transparent, publicly accountable, and trustworthy—readers demand a visible, responsible presence they can rely on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as teachers: social responsibility and moral tone
rubrics_metrics.description: “The daily journal is destined, if it survives as a power, to become the teacher—the very Bible—of the people. The people are already beginning to distinguish between the wholesome and the meretricious in their newspapers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should recognize the educative power of the press and aim to produce wholesome, constructive content; proprietors and editors must value character and avoid pandering to meretricious influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism, 'scoops' and stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Too often the newspaper subaltern obtaining promotion... has been too busy seeking 'scoops' and doing 'stunts' to concern himself about perspectives, principles, causes and effects...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist chasing ephemeral scoops and sensational stunts at the expense of thoughtful perspective; prioritize principles, analysis of causes and effects, and the probable impressions and consequences of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of formal training and mastery of fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is room for special training toward the making of an editor... The School of Journalism may not be always able to give him the needful instruction. But it can set him in the right direction and better prepare him to think and act for himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional education can provide the rudiments—technical details, perspective, and critical habits—that on-the-job experience alone may miss; training should prepare journalists to think independently and responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical analogy to illuminate modern issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazlitt uses Tarifa and the Moors as an historical origin to explain the roots of modern protective/tariff systems and 'Robber Barons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing vivid historical examples or analogies (e.g., Tarif‑Ben‑Malik and Spanish piracy) can make abstract or contemporary political/economic critiques more concrete and rhetorically forceful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evocative descriptive detail and anecdote in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations such as the Galt House stories, the Seville 'House of Pontius Pilate', and vivid character sketches are used to convey place and people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring scenes and characters alive with concrete, sometimes amusing anecdotes and local particulars; travel and social description succeed by naming objects, telling stories, and offering sensory detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character depiction: bully/braggart as a recognizable type
rubrics_metrics.description: “The son-of-a-gun from Bitter Creek... He is not always a coward. Driven, as it were, to the wall, he will often make good.” (Detailed behaviors: boasts, seeks 'free fight', then withdraws.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting bullies or braggarts, use stock behaviors (boasting, seeking adventures, bluster that often conceals timidity) and short illustrative episodes to render the type believable and often comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show social consequences of rumor and appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ellen Godwin / John Throckmorton story shows how public appearances and gossip ruined an otherwise honorable man's prospects and happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anecdotes that demonstrate how public perception and scandal (even when unfounded) can affect reputation and life; depict how communities accept appearances and judge swiftly to dramatize social dynamics.
